title_en: E. I. du Pont de Nemours and Company v. Beijing Guowang Information Co., Ltd. — dispute over infringement of computer network domain name

full_text_en:
E. I. du Pont de Nemours and Company v. Beijing Guowang Information Co., Ltd. — dispute over Internet domain name infringement and unfair competition

Plaintiff: E. I. du Pont de Nemours and Company, domiciled at 1007 Market Street, Wilmington, Delaware, United States.
Legal representative: Calissa W. Brown, authorized representative.
Agent ad litem: Shao Wei and Shen Chunxiang, trademark agents of China Patent & Trademark Agent (H.K.) Ltd.

Defendant: Beijing Guowang Information Co., Ltd., domiciled at Dongzhimen South Street, Dongcheng District, Beijing.
Legal representative: Zhao Huimin, Chairman of the Board of the company.
Agent ad litem: Shu Ziping and Yuan Feng, attorneys at Beijing Beige Law Firm.

The Plaintiff, E. I. du Pont de Nemours and Company, initiated an action against the Defendant, Beijing Guowang Information Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Guowang Company), for Internet domain name trademark infringement and unfair competition before the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court.

The Plaintiff alleged: Our company, with a history of 200 years, is currently one of the 500 largest enterprises in the world and has long had trade relations with China. The oval font “DU PONT” trademark we use and register, although not formally recognized as a well-known trademark through administrative procedures, has in fact become a well-known trademark due to our high-quality products and high-level services. It should be entitled to comprehensive cross-class protection across different goods and services, including protection in the field of Internet domain names. The Defendant, as an information company and domain name service provider, knowing that registering a domain name using another's business name or trademark name is improper, nonetheless unauthorizedly used our trademark name to register a domain name and, despite our repeated requests, intentionally retained that domain name. Our customers identify our company and products by the name “dupont.” On the Internet, they will also attempt to contact us through “dupont.com.” However, when Chinese customers input “dupont.com.cn,” they only see a blank page. The Defendant's conduct not only prevents us from registering the domain name “dupont.com.cn” but also causes confusion and misidentification among customers, harming our goodwill and customer relations. Pursuant to the Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property (hereinafter the Paris Convention), the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter the General Principles of Civil Law), the Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter the Trademark Law), and the Anti-Unfair Competition Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter the Anti-Unfair Competition Law), the Defendant's conduct constitutes trademark infringement and unfair competition. We request the court to order the Defendant to: 1. Immediately cancel the domain name “dupont.com.cn” registered with the China Internet Network Information Center to cease the infringement of our exclusive right to use the “DU PONT” trademark and the unfair competition; 2. Publicly apologize to us in a newspaper; 3. Bear the investigation and evidence collection costs of RMB 2,700 incurred by us for this lawsuit.

The Defendant argued: 1. This case does not fall within the scope of civil litigation. The Defendant obtained the dupont domain name as a result of a specific administrative licensing act by the domain name administrative authority. If that administrative act is unlawful and infringes the Plaintiff's lawful rights, and if the dispute cannot be resolved through administrative objection procedures, the Plaintiff should file an administrative lawsuit against the China Internet Network Information Center as the defendant; 2. The Plaintiff's “DU PONT” trademark has not been recognized as a well-known trademark through administrative procedures and therefore is not a well-known trademark; 3. Trademarks and domain names are entirely different concepts in different fields. The registration and use of Internet domain names are not within the scope of regulation under the Trademark Law, and the specific acts of trademark infringement enumerated in the Trademark Law do not include the act of registering a domain name identical to another's registered trademark; 4. The Defendant's registration of the domain name “dupont.com.cn” cannot possibly lead to confusion regarding the Plaintiff's goods. This conduct does not constitute unfair competition under the Paris Convention or the Anti-Unfair Competition Law. The Plaintiff's allegations of trademark infringement and unfair competition are without factual or legal basis, and the court should dismiss the Plaintiff's complaint.

The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court found the following facts after trial:

The Plaintiff, E. I. du Pont de Nemours and Company, was incorporated in the United States in 1802. Its products now cover electronics, automobiles, apparel, construction, transportation, communications, agriculture, household products, chemicals, and other fields, and are sold in more than 150 countries and regions. Since its establishment, the Plaintiff has consistently used the oval font “DU PONT” on its products as an identifier of the manufacturer. In 1921, the Plaintiff first registered the oval font “DUPONT” as a trademark in the United States for goods in Classes 1, 2, 3, 5, 9, 13, and 17; subsequently, it registered the trademark in 94 countries, regions, and organizations, including Brazil, Germany, Denmark, France, India, Japan, and the African Intellectual Property Organization, covering dozens of goods classes such as Classes 1, 3, 122, 23, and 24.

From November 1986 to the present, the Plaintiff, through successive assignments and registrations with the Trademark Office of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce (hereinafter the Trademark Office), acquired the exclusive right to use the registered oval font “DU PONT” trademark for goods in Classes 3, 11, 22, 24, 26, 30, and 31. The Plaintiff continuously promoted the oval font “DU PONT” trademark in mainland China through the production of television specials, participation in special exhibitions, product seminars, and advertising in media. In 1997, the Plaintiff spent USD 1,482,000 on advertising for this purpose, and in the same year, sales of goods using this trademark in China amounted to USD 223,000,000.

From November 1986 to the present, the Plaintiff, through successive assignments and registrations with the Trademark Office, acquired the exclusive right to use the registered Chinese character trademark “杜邦” for goods in Classes 23, 26, 30, 31, and 46.

In February 1999, the Plaintiff also registered the word mark “DUPONT” with the Trademark Office, approved for use on goods in Class 21. On April 1, the “DUPONT” word mark was included in the “National Key Trademark Protection List” compiled by the Trademark Office.

The third-level domain names registered by the Plaintiff in 17 countries, including the United States, Germany, Canada, and Russia, all follow the pattern of “dupont.com.[administrative region abbreviation]” or “dupont.[administrative region abbreviation]” or “dupont.co.[administrative region abbreviation].”

The Defendant, Guowang Company, was incorporated in March 1996, with a business scope including computer network information consulting services, computer network online services, and technical development of computer software and hardware. On November 2, 1998, the company registered the domain name “dupont.com.cn” with the China Internet Network Information Center and has never actually used it to date.

In March 1999, the Plaintiff's subsidiary in China, DuPont China Limited, sent a letter to the Defendant, Guowang Company, stating: “We have noted that you have registered the domain name ‘dupont.com.cn’ in the People's Republic of China. DuPont has been engaged in international commercial activities under the DUPONT trademark for nearly 200 years and is the registered owner of the DUPONT trademark (including the oval logo) in various countries around the world. Our company has more than 10 wholly-owned or joint ventures in China, all registered under the name ‘DUPONT.’ We have also registered the ‘DUPONT’ trademark in China. Our domain name in the United States and other countries is DUPONT.COM. We demand that you immediately cease using the DUPONT domain name and immediately cancel the registration of ‘dupont.com.cn.’”

On November 4, 1999, entrusted by the Plaintiff, Hong Kong China Patent & Trademark Agent (H.K.) Ltd. applied to the Beijing Notary Public Office to notarize the web pages of the Defendant, Guowang Company, on the Internet. The notarization proved that the web pages of Guowang Company contained the following text: “A domain name is a company's ‘trademark’ on the Internet and is the most important clue for other enterprise users to identify and access a company's website. From a business perspective, a domain name has been hailed as a company's ‘online trademark,’ and failing to register a domain name is more troublesome than having a trademark hijacked. Guowang Company provides a complete set of enterprise informatization solutions, including domain name registration and virtual hosting, to assist enterprises in implementing e-commerce.” The web page also listed the conditions for registering a domain name, including the requirement that “no one else's enterprise name or trademark name that has been registered in China may be used.”

The Plaintiff incurred investigation and evidence collection costs of RMB 2,700 for this lawsuit.

During the trial, the Defendant, Guowang Company, could not demonstrate any connection between its name, address, abbreviation, logo, business, or any other aspect and the term “dupont.”

The above facts are confirmed by the following evidence: the trademark registration certificates for the “DU PONT” word mark and oval font mark; the letter from DuPont China Limited to Guowang Company; the Plaintiff's advertisements; Notarial Certificates (99) Jing Zheng Jing Zi Nos. 31435 and 31436; Domain Name Registration Certificate No. 981102005077; the Plaintiff's application for well-known trademark recognition submitted to the Trademark Office and its attachments; the registration certificate for the “杜邦” trademark; the Trademark Office's trademark notice; and statements of both parties. All evidence has been subjected to cross-examination and verification and may serve as the basis for establishing the facts of this case.

The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court held:

The Plaintiff, E. I. du Pont de Nemours and Company, alleges that the Defendant, Guowang Company, has infringed its trademark rights and engaged in unfair competition, and requests that the court hold Guowang Company civilly liable under the Paris Convention and Chinese law to protect the Plaintiff's civil rights. Therefore, this case is a civil rights dispute and falls within the scope of civil litigation accepted by the People's Courts. The Defendant's argument that this case is not a civil lawsuit and that the Plaintiff should file an administrative lawsuit is without legal basis and is not supported.

The Plaintiff, incorporated in the United States, is a U.S. legal person. Both China and the United States are members of the Paris Convention, so this case shall be governed by Chinese law and the provisions of the Paris Convention.

Since 1921, the Plaintiff's oval font “DU PONT” trademark has been registered in 94 countries, regions, or organizations. Due to the Plaintiff's high product quality and its extensive, sustained, and large-scale advertising over many years, the Plaintiff has built a huge user base worldwide, and the volume of goods sold under the oval font “DUPONT” trademark is substantial. The oval font “DU PONT” trademark was registered in China in 1976, and the Plaintiff enjoys an exclusive right to use it. The Plaintiff has also made substantial advertising expenditures in China, and goods bearing the oval font “DU PONT” trademark have a large number of consumers in China. China has become an important market for the Plaintiff's products, and the oval font “DU PONT” trademark enjoys a high reputation in the Chinese market and is well known to the relevant public in China. In light of the above facts, the Plaintiff's assertion that the oval font “DU PONT” trademark is in fact a well-known trademark should be upheld.

Whether a trademark is well-known is an objective fact. The determination of a well-known trademark essentially constitutes a confirmation of an objective fact concerning civil rights. Therefore, the People's Court has the authority to determine whether a trademark involved in a case is well-known. The Defendant's argument that the oval font “DU PONT” trademark has not been recognized as a well-known trademark through administrative procedures and therefore is not a well-known trademark is without legal basis and is not supported.

The Paris Convention establishes a protection system for well-known trademarks. As a well-known trademark, the oval font “DU PONT” trademark involved in this case should receive special protection at a higher level than that generally afforded to ordinary trademarks. The essence of protecting well-known trademarks is to prohibit others from using them commercially in any form without authorization. Because well-known trademarks enjoy considerable recognition, even if used on goods or services that are not similar, such use may lead the public to mistakenly believe that the source of those goods or services has some connection with the well-known trademark, thereby causing confusion and diluting the distinctiveness of the well-known trademark and damaging its goodwill. Therefore, the protection of well-known trademarks should be understood to extend to goods or services that are not similar to those for which the trademark is registered or actually used.

In recent years, the Internet has developed rapidly around the world and has become an indispensable tool for the survival and development of enterprises. The Internet is characterized by fast transmission and wide coverage. This characteristic can be used to more promptly and fully realize lawful rights and interests, but it can also allow unlawful acts to produce more rapid and severe harmful consequences. Therefore, it is necessary to grant well-known trademarks special protection on the Internet—higher than that afforded to ordinary trademarks—so as to prevent damage to the distinctiveness and goodwill of well-known trademarks.

A domain name is a name and address on the Internet for an Internet user. A domain name has an identifying function and serves as a sign representing the domain name registrant on the Internet. Because domain names are highly distinctive, Internet visitors generally rely on domain names to distinguish information service providers, and domain names are increasingly becoming important identifiers for enterprises on the Internet. This characteristic gives domain names significant intellectual property significance in the commercial field; enterprises often endeavor to use their trademarks or trade names as domain names so that visitors can identify the goods and services of the website creator through the domain name. Using a well-known trademark as a domain name also allows for commercial promotion by leveraging the fame and reputation of the well-known trademark to attract customers and achieve a high hit rate. The owner of a trademark right should have the right to use its well-known trademark in the form of a domain name and enjoy the benefits derived from the well-known trademark on the Internet. Consequently, the act of registering another's well-known trademark as a domain name necessarily harms the lawful rights and interests of the trademark owner.

The word mark “DU PONT” is the most important part of the Plaintiff's oval font “DUPONT” well-known trademark. The Defendant, Guowang Company, cannot explain any connection between its name, address, abbreviation, logo, business, or any other aspect and the term “dupont,” nor can it prove that it enjoys a prior right to use the term “dupont” in the domain name field. Nevertheless, it took the most distinctive element of the Plaintiff's well-known trademark and registered the domain name “dupont.com.cn.” If the domain name registered by Guowang Company were put into use on the Internet, it would inevitably blur the distinction between the domain name and the “DU PONT” trademark, causing confusion among the public. In fact, after registering “dupont.com.cn” as a domain name, Guowang Company did not use it; it merely served to prevent the Plaintiff from registering it as a domain name, obstructing the Plaintiff's ability to use its own trademark in commercial activities on the Chinese Internet.

Article 38, paragraph (4) of the Trademark Law promulgated on September 2, 1993, designates acts that “otherwise cause damage to the exclusive right to use a registered trademark” as acts infringing the exclusive right to use a registered trademark. The Defendant, Guowang Company, as an agent for domain name registration, knows to advise its clients that “no one else's enterprise name or trademark name that has been registered in China may be used” when acting on their behalf in domain name registration, yet it itself registered the Plaintiff's well-known trademark name as a domain name. From this, it can be seen that Guowang Company acted with malice in registering the domain name “dupont.com.cn,” and this act has in fact resulted in hindering the Plaintiff from using its well-known trademark in commercial activities on the Chinese Internet. Guowang Company's conduct constitutes infringement of the Plaintiff's exclusive right to use its well-known trademark. Article 4 of the General Principles of Civil Law provides: “Civil activities shall be conducted in accordance with the principles of voluntariness, fairness, making compensation for equal value, honesty, and good faith.” Article 2, paragraph 1 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law similarly provides: “Operators in market transactions shall follow the principles of voluntariness, equality, fairness, honesty, and good faith, and comply with recognized commercial ethics.” Guowang Company maliciously registered the Plaintiff's well-known trademark as a domain name, appropriated another's goodwill without compensation for its own improper benefit, and, even after receiving a warning letter from the Plaintiff's Chinese subsidiary, failed to rectify this improper conduct. This violates the principle of honesty and good faith and also constitutes unfair competition. Guowang Company shall bear civil liability for infringement, including ceasing the infringement and compensating the Plaintiff for the investigation and evidence collection costs incurred in this lawsuit. Since Guowang Company did not actually use the registered domain name, the Plaintiff's request for a public apology is not supported.

In conclusion, the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court rendered judgment on November 21, 2000, as follows:

1. The Defendant, Guowang Company, shall, within ten days from the effective date of this judgment, cancel its registered domain name “dupont.com.cn”;
2. The Defendant, Guowang Company, shall, within thirty days from the effective date of this judgment, pay the Plaintiff, E. I. du Pont de Nemours and Company, compensation in the amount of RMB 2,700 for the investigation and evidence collection costs incurred in this lawsuit;
3. The Plaintiff's other claims are dismissed.

After the first-instance judgment was announced, Guowang Company appealed to the Beijing High People's Court, arguing: The first-instance court's determination that domain names fall within the scope of intellectual property and that the trademark owner has the right to use its well-known trademark in the form of a domain name has no legal basis; the domain name registered by the appellant is only used in computer networks and would not cause confusion concerning the source of the public; the appellant did not obstruct the appellee from using its own trademark in commercial activities on computer networks; the appellant's lack of connection with “dupont” in terms of name, address, or other aspects cannot be used to infer malice; the appellant did not use the appellee's goodwill to obtain improper benefit; the appellant did not violate Article 4 of the General Principles of Civil Law, Article 38, paragraph (4) of the Trademark Law, Article 2, paragraph 1 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law, or Article 4 of the Paris Convention. The first-instance court's application of the above laws and international conventions in rendering its judgment was erroneous.

E. I. du Pont de Nemours and Company complied with the first-instance judgment.

During the second-instance proceedings, the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Civil Disputes over Domain Names on Computer Networks (Fa Shi [2001] No. 24) came into effect on July 24, 2001 (see Issue No. 4, 2001 of this Gazette). Article 8 thereof provides: “If the People's Court determines that an act of domain name registration or use constitutes infringement or unfair competition, it may order the defendant to cease the infringement, cancel the domain name, or, upon the plaintiff's request, order that the plaintiff register and use the domain name; if actual damage has been caused to the right holder, the court may order the defendant to pay damages.”

The Beijing High People's Court, after trial, held that the facts found in the first instance judgment were clear and the application of law was correct. Article 8 of Judicial Interpretation Fa Shi [2001] No. 24 provides that, "where it is determined that the act of registering or using a domain name constitutes infringement or unfair competition, the defendant may be ordered to cease the infringement and cancel the domain name." The first count of the judgment at first instance ordered Guowang Company to "revoke its registered domain name 'dupont.com.cn'." Although the phrasing differs, the intent is consistent. Moreover, this judgment was rendered prior to the announcement and implementation of the said judicial interpretation, and therefore no change is made. Accordingly, the Beijing High People's Court, in accordance with Article 153, Paragraph 1, Item (1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered judgment on November 15, 2001:

Appeal dismissed, original judgment affirmed.
